replacement: Now it is an unquestionable fact that people who know both kinds of pleasure equally well, and are equally able to appreciate and enjoy both, markedly prefer the way of life that engages their higher faculties. Few human creatures would accept being turned into one of the lower animals, even for a promise of the fullest share of a beast's pleasures. No intelligent person would agree to be a fool, no instructed person an ignoramus, no person of feeling and conscience selfish and base, even if convinced that the fool, the dunce, or the rascal is better satisfied with his lot than they are with theirs. They would not trade away what they have beyond what he has, not even for the complete satisfaction of every desire they share with him. If they ever imagine they would, it is only in a state of unhappiness so extreme that they would swap their lot for almost any other to escape it, however undesirable they found that other lot. A being with higher faculties needs more in order to be happy, is probably able to suffer more acutely, and is certainly exposed to suffering at more points than a being of an inferior type. Despite all this, he can never truly wish to sink into what he feels to be a lower grade of existence. We may explain this unwillingness however we like. We may put it down to pride, a name that gets applied without distinction to some of the most and some of the least estimable feelings mankind has. We may trace it to the love of liberty and personal independence, which the Stoics appealed to as one of the most effective ways of teaching it; or to the love of power, or to the love of excitement, both of which really do play a part in it. But the name that fits it best is a sense of dignity. Every human being has this in one form or another, and in some it matches their higher faculties, though by no means exactly. For those in whom it is strong, it is so essential a part of their happiness that nothing in conflict with it could attract them, except for a moment. Anyone who supposes that this preference costs the superior being some happiness — that he is not happier than the inferior one in anything like equal circumstances — is confounding two very different ideas, happiness and content. It is indisputable that a being with low capacities for enjoyment has the best chance of satisfying them fully, while a highly endowed being will always feel that whatever happiness he can look for, in the world as it is, is imperfect. But he can learn to put up with its imperfections, if they are at all bearable. And they will not make him envy the being who is unconscious of them, since that being is unconscious only because he does not feel at all the good which those imperfections qualify. It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question. The other party to the comparison knows both sides.
